ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Each participating site will obtain local ethics approval for collecting, anonymizing, and publicly sharing data.
The original study by Eimer et al. (2003) employed a within-subject design in which 14 participants completed two tasks (emotion and line tasks).
table.formatted: The original study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref> employed a within-subject design in which 14 participants completed two tasks (emotion and line tasks).

table.text: In the emotion task, participants were asked to discriminate between neutral faces and emotional faces (laterally presented to the left and right of the fixation point) showing one of the six basic emotions (disgusted, fearful, happy, sad, surprised, angry) in each block.
In the line task, participants were asked to judge the length of line segments closer to the central fixation while viewing the same face displays.
If any participants are to be excluded from the analysis, more participants will be tested to replace the excluded participants to obtain usable data from 41 participants in each replicating lab.

Volunteers are eligible for the study if they are 1) aged 18-60 years, 2) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, 3) self-reporting to have no neurological condition, and 4) without any skin allergies.
If more than 50% of epochs in any of the two tasks from a participant are to be removed by this step, this particular participant will be removed from any further analysis.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> The original study by Eimer et al. (2003) employed a within-subject design in which 14 participants completed two tasks (emotion and line tasks).

> In the emotion task, participants were asked to discriminate between neutral faces and emotional faces (laterally presented to the left and right of the fixation point) showing one of the six basic emotions (disgusted, fearful, happy, sad, surprised, angry) in each block.

> In the line task, participants were asked to judge the length of line segments closer to the central fixation while viewing the same face displays.

> If any participants are to be excluded from the analysis, more participants will be tested to replace the excluded participants to obtain usable data from 41 participants in each replicating lab.

> Volunteers are eligible for the study if they are 1) aged 18-60 years, 2) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, 3) self-reporting to have no neurological condition, and 4) without any skin allergies.

> If more than 50% of epochs in any of the two tasks from a participant are to be removed by this step, this particular participant will be removed from any further analysis.

Ethics approval statement:

> Each participating site will obtain local ethics approval for collecting, anonymizing, and publicly sharing data.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Following the #EEGManyLabs recommendations (Pavlov et al., 2021) and recognizing that ERP studies often overestimate effect sizes due to small samples (Clayson et al., 2019), we calculated the required sample size of the replication. The calculation was based on the weakest original significant Task x Emotion interaction found in 160-215 ms (F = 5.2, corresponding to η² p = 0.2857). We targeted 90% power to detect an effect half of the original effect (i.e., η² p = 0.1429) at an alpha level of .02. With these settings, an a priori power analysis using MorePower 6.0.4 (Campbell & Thompson, 2012) indicated a sample size of 82.

Following the decision to reduce the sample size per replicating lab from 82 to 41, we did a sensitivity power analysis using MorePower 6.0.4 to assess the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) that each replicating lab can achieve for the Task x Emotion interactions. With 90% power and an alpha level of .02, the analysis showed an MDES of η² p = 0.2587. This effect size is smaller than that of the weakest significant Task x Emotion interaction in the original study (frontal positivity at 160-215 ms, η² p = 0.2857). Expressed as power, each replicating lab will have 94.3% power to detect an effect of the magnitude reported for the weakest original interaction, and 98.9% and 99.9% power for the effects reported in the 220-315 ms and the later time windows. By comparison, the original study, with N = 14 and an alpha level of .05, could only reliably detect effects of η² p = 0.468 or larger at 90% power. Therefore, even with the halved sample size, each replicating lab is about twice as sensitive as the study being replicated, and at a more stringent alpha level. Furthermore, the metaanalysis will be highly powered. The replication study has eight participating labs so far, giving a total sample size of 328. With this pooled sample size, at 90% power and alpha level of .02, we will be able to detect the effect as small as η² p = 0.0386 (a small effect size). Eimer et al. (2003) did not find any difference in the N170 component, neither did they observe any differences across the six basic emotions. While it is widely accepted that emotional faces elicit enhanced ERP responses in comparison to neutral faces as found in the original study (e.g., Leppänen et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2010; Smith, 2012), whether these effects require focal attention remains a topic of debate. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > .02", "p > .02 "), Sentence = c("For each negative hypothesis, we define successful replication as a non-significant meta-analytic estimate (p > .02).", "f The symbol '-' denotes results of p > .02 or BF10 ≤ 0.333." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. #### Package Installation (install.packages)

Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). #### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 12 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: Each participating site will obtain local ethics approval for collecting, anonymizing, and publicly sharing data.
live_data_statements: The original study by Eimer et al. (2003) employed a within-subject design in which 14 participants completed two tasks (emotion and line tasks).

In the emotion task, participants were asked to discriminate between neutral faces and emotional faces (laterally presented to the left and right of the fixation point) showing one of the six basic emotions (disgusted, fearful, happy, sad, surprised, angry) in each block.
In the line task, participants were asked to judge the length of line segments closer to the central fixation while viewing the same face displays.
If any participants are to be excluded from the analysis, more participants will be tested to replace the excluded participants to obtain usable data from 41 participants in each replicating lab.

Volunteers are eligible for the study if they are 1) aged 18-60 years, 2) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, 3) self-reporting to have no neurological condition, and 4) without any skin allergies.
If more than 50% of epochs in any of the two tasks from a participant are to be removed by this step, this particular participant will be removed from any further analysis.

report: ### Python code
This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 Python code files.
#### Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no `source()`-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an `import` loads a module, not the paper's own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:3, File = c("Practice task1.py", "Practice task2.py", 
"FacialExpression.py"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—"), 
    Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", "none")), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 3 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Practice task1.py", "Practice task2.py", 
"FacialExpression.py"), Outcome = c("dependency_unavailable", 
"dependency_unavailable", "dependency_unavailable"), Detail = c("dependency_unavailable", 
"dependency_unavailable", "dependency_unavailable"), "Time (s)" = c(1, 
0.9, 1)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Dependency-unavailable errors**

**3 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to `pip install`. This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Practice task1.py", "Practice task2.py", 
"FacialExpression.py")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`os.chdir()` in the code**

**3 scripts call `os.chdir()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with `pass`. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring an `os.chdir()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("FacialExpression.py", "Practice task1.py", 
"Practice task2.py"), "os.chdir() removed" = c(1L, 1L, 1L), "Path(s) it set" = c("(non-literal)", 
"(non-literal)", "(non-literal)")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

text.text: How the brain processes facial expressions and whether this process requires focal attention have been central topics of neurophysiological research on face processing.

In a seminal study, using scalp-recorded event-related potentials (ERPs), Eimer, Holmes, and McGlone (2003) found that emotional and neutral faces were differently processed in the brain as early as 160 ms after stimulus onset.
text.formatted: In a seminal study, using scalp-recorded event-related potentials (ERPs), Eimer, Holmes, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">McGlone (2003)</ref> found that emotional and neutral faces were differently processed in the brain as early as 160 ms after stimulus onset.

text.text: Importantly, these ERP differences disappeared when attention was directed away from the face stimuli, suggesting the necessity of focal attention in facial expression processing.
These results have greatly motivated further research in the field.
Yet, subsequent research did not always agree with these findings, and the study was never directly replicated.
Hence, this study has been selected by #EEGManyLabs, a global and multi-laboratory replication project, for a high-powered direct replication across multiple laboratories (N = 41 in each laboratory).
We hypothesize the replication of the original positive findings, including the ERP effects differentiating emotional and neutral faces and their dependence on focal attention.

To address the debate on facial expression processing and the role of N170, we will also take this opportunity to reassess key negative findings of the original study, namely no difference between emotional and neutral facial expressions in N170 and no ERP differences among the six facial expressions.
Replication or revision of these findings will confirm the necessity of focal attention in emotional face processing and the postulated biomarkers of basic emotion processing.
This study will provide a reproducible benchmark on face processing.
The ability to process facial expressions rapidly and accurately is central to human social communication (Anderson & Phelps, 2001; Fox et al., 2000; Öhman et al., 2001).
text.formatted: The ability to process facial expressions rapidly and accurately is central to human social communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson & Phelps, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Fox et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Öhman et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Faces convey critical information about another's emotional state and intentions, and the way the brain responds to these visual cues has been a topic of extensive research over the past few decades (Ekman, Friesen, & Ellsworth, 1972; Niedenthal & Ric, 2017).

text.text: Furthermore, research has also been trying to determine whether focal attention is needed for facial expression processing, which represents the level of automaticity in perceiving emotion in faces (Pessoa et al., 2002; Vuilleumier et al., 2001).

text.text: A seminal study in this field by Eimer, Holmes, and McGlone (2003) demonstrated that several scalp-recorded event-related potential (ERP) activities (as early as 160 ms after stimulus onset) distinguished between laterally presented neutral and emotional faces when visual attention was allocated to faces.
text.formatted: A seminal study in this field by <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer, Holmes, and McGlone (2003)</ref> demonstrated that several scalp-recorded event-related potential (ERP) activities (as early as 160 ms after stimulus onset) distinguished between laterally presented neutral and emotional faces when visual attention was allocated to faces.

text.text: More importantly, they also showed that the effect disappeared when attention was diverted by a demanding perceptual task.

The findings suggested the necessity of focal attention in processing of facial expressions (e.g., Pessoa et al., 2002) and challenged the notion that emotional face processing occurs pre-attentively (e.g., Vuilleumier et al., 2001).

text.text: The work by Eimer et al. (2003) was among the first to demonstrate that attention modulates the neural processing of emotional faces (i.e., the attention-gating account of emotional face processing), and it has shaped much of the subsequent empirical and theoretical landscape.

text.text: After 23 years of its publication, Eimer et al. (2003) still remained a classic study and has consistently been cited throughout the years.

However, the findings of the Eimer et al. (2003) study have been often debated upon.

text.text: While it is widely accepted that emotional faces elicit enhanced ERP responses in comparison to neutral faces as found in the original study (e.g., Leppänen et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2010; Smith, 2012), whether these effects require focal attention remains a topic of debate.

text.text: More crucially, the absence of any difference in the N170 component (a biomarker of early structural encoding of face stimuli; e.g., Bentin et al., 1996), both between emotional and neutral faces and among the six emotions, have been questioned in later research.

text.text: The original study by Eimer et al. (2003) employed a within-subject design in which 14 participants completed two tasks (emotion and line tasks).
text.formatted: The original study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref> employed a within-subject design in which 14 participants completed two tasks (emotion and line tasks).

text.text: In the emotion task, participants were asked to discriminate between neutral faces and emotional faces (laterally presented to the left and right of the fixation point) showing one of the six basic emotions (disgusted, fearful, happy, sad, surprised, angry) in each block.
In the line task, participants were asked to judge the length of line segments closer to the central fixation while viewing the same face displays.
This perceptual task demanded visuospatial attention away from the face stimuli.

Their results showed ERP differences between the neutral and emotional face conditions (termed "valence effect" in the original publication; we changed this term to "emotion effect" in the current study given that this effect could also relate to arousal; Russell,1980), and more importantly, the modulation of the emotion effect by the involvement of focal attention.
text.formatted: Their results showed ERP differences between the neutral and emotional face conditions (termed "valence effect" in the original publication; we changed this term to "emotion effect" in the current study given that this effect could also relate to arousal; <ref type="bibr">Russell,1980)</ref>, and more importantly, the modulation of the emotion effect by the involvement of focal attention.

text.text: With focal attention (emotion task), significant ERP differences were found between emotional and neutral faces (not differentiating among the six emotions) at four time windows over frontal, central, temporal, and occipital scalp regions (with the earliest window being 160-215 ms in the frontal area).
However, no such difference was found when focal attention was directed away from faces.

These results contradicted the basic emotion theories, which suggest that the basic emotions are rapidly detected by automatic and distinct neural mechanisms operating independently of the involvement of voluntary attention (Ekman, 1992; Ortony & Turner, 1990).

text.text: Furthermore, there were two noteworthy non-significant results in Eimer et al. (2003) -there was no emotion effect in the N170 component, and no difference among the six basic emotions either.

text.text: The absence of the emotion effect in N170 agreed with the Bruce and Young model in that structural encoding of faces (represented by the N170 component; Bentin et al., 1996; Bentin & Deouell, 2000) and the processing of emotional facial expressions are separate processes in the brain (Bruce & Young, 1986; Eimer, 2011).

text.text: According to the Bruce and Young model (1986), the first stage of face processing is structural encoding, which derives a description of the face structure.

text.text: The encoded face structure will then be fed into parallel and independent routes of identity processing (for familiar faces) and non-identity processing (for unfamiliar faces).
A face's emotional state is analysed in the non-identity route after structural encoding (see also Lander & Butcher, 2015; Young, 2018).

text.text: The absence of any difference among the emotions suggests that facial expression is processed in the same manner in neocortex and with the same time course.
In short, the findings of Eimer et al. (2003) can be summarized in four aspects.
text.formatted: In short, the findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref> can be summarized in four aspects.

text.text: The first is the presence of emotion effects (enhanced processing of emotional faces relative to neutral faces) in several ERP activities with focal attention allocated to faces.
The second is the absence of these emotion effects with focal attention directed away from faces.
The third is the absence of any emotion effect in N170.
And the last aspect is the absence of any difference among the six emotions.

The first aspect has been consistently supported by later research, which showed the emotion effect over several comparable time periods and scalps regions (e.g., Bar-Haim et al., 2005; Leppänen et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The first aspect has been consistently supported by later research, which showed the emotion effect over several comparable time periods and scalps regions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bar-Haim et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Leppänen et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Luo et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: However, the other three aspects have been heavily debated in the literature.
The debate regarding the second aspect (i.e., absence of emotion effects without focal attention) has been focusing on the level of automaticity of emotional face processing.
Research carried out around the time of Eimer et al. (2003) agreed with the original study.

text.text: For instance, Holmes, Vuilleumier, and Eimer (2003) showed participants arrays containing two faces and two houses, with faces displaying either a fearful or neutral expression.

text.text: Spatial attention was directed to the faces or houses.
Results showed stronger frontal positivity (approximately 100 ms post-stimulus) for fearful faces relative to neutral faces when attention was directed to faces.
Just as Eimer et al. (2003) showed, this difference was absent when attention was paid to the houses.

text.text: Additionally, the result was also confirmed by Holmes, Winston, and Eimer (2005), who demonstrated the same presence and absence of emotion effect respectively with and without focal attention on faces.

text.text: Conversely, the emotion effect was totally absent in spatially filtered face stimuli.
As such, around that time, it was concluded that emotional face processing is not fully automatic and is modulated by attentional manipulations (e.g., Palermo & Rhodes, 2007; Pessoa, 2005).

text.text: However, it soon turned out that the automaticity level of emotional face processing may depend on the location of face stimulus presentation.
The evidence supporting Eimer et al. (2003) all came from studies presenting face stimuli laterally (to the left and right of the fixation).

text.text: In contrast, the literature started to show that early emotion-related processing appears to proceed automatically when faces are presented at the location of the fixation point. Holmes, Kiss, and Eimer (2006) presented face stimuli at the fixation, and found that the initial stage of emotional face processing (160-220 ms) occurred even when spatial attention was directed to a line task (for a review, see Eimer & Holmes, 2007).

text.text: While centrally presented faces can elicit early, pre-attentive responses, later sustained processing, including early posterior negativity (EPN, which represents an early attention mechanism enhancing brain responses to emotional information; Schindler et al., 2019; Schupp et al., 2006) and late positive potential (LPP, which indexes emotional stimulus evaluation and attentional control; Schindler et al., 2019; Schupp et al., 2006), may still require focused attention.

text.text: A critical counterargument to the notion of fully automatic processing of emotional face stimuli (centrally presented) is that some residual attention may still be available for the processing, if the non-face tasks used in the studies above were not difficult enough to totally deplete the attentional resources (e.g., Pessoa et al., 2002).

text.text: This counterargument is especially noteworthy given that object identification is typically associated with foveal processing, which differs from and probably runs in parallel to peripheral processing (Ludwig et al., 2014).

text.text: To test this counterargument, Schindler et al. (2021) presented stimuli at fixation and manipulated the perceptual load of the non-face task to assess the amount of residual attention needed for the emotional face processing, as high perceptual load tasks can effectively exhaust attentional resources available for other processes (Lavie, 2005).

text.text: They found that the emotion effects in early ERP activities (P1 and N170) were not modulated by load, whereas the later effect in EPN was dependent on attention.
Together, these findings suggest that the earliest stages of facial expression analysis operate without capacity limits, whereas subsequent processing remains attention bounded.

The combined evidence (presentation location and perceptual load manipulation) suggests that the level of automaticity decreases for early processing of emotional faces with lateral stimulus presentation in comparison to presentation at fixation.

This central-peripheral dissociation is especially noteworthy because Eimer et al. (2003) placed their faces in the parafovea (2.2° from fixation centre-to-centre, 3.4° to the far edges) -an eccentricity that retains considerably higher acuity than the periphery which is beyond 5° from fixation (Larson & Loschky, 2009; Rayner, 1998) yet is already subject to attentional gating. Eimer et al.'s (2003) results thus mark a boundary between foveal and peripheral emotion processing.

text.text: Taken into consideration of all the empirical evidence discussed above (i.e., lateral vs. foveal image presentation, attention modulation by non-face tasks, and perceptual load manipulation), several theoretical accounts were developed to characterize the graded effects of attention on emotional face processing. Pessoa (2008) and Pessoa and Adolphs (2010) proposed multiple levels of automaticity: subcortical routes can trigger rapid affective responses even when attention is limited, whereas ERP components that originate from cortical structures (such as P1 and N170) are modulated by available attentional resources. Luo et al. (2010) further suggested that coarse detection of some negative emotions (especially fear) can occur automatically in early neural responses (e.g., P1), while precise categorization requires attentional investment.

(2010)</ref> further suggested that coarse detection of some negative emotions (especially fear) can occur automatically in early neural responses (e.g., P1), while precise categorization requires attentional investment.

text.text: A review by Schindler and Bublatzky (2020) concurs: early responses are typically attention-independent, whereas sustained engagement with emotional content, particularly for complex or subtle expressions, depends on focal attention.
This body of work therefore converges on a dual-process view: rapid, automatic detection of emotional salience is followed by attention-dependent elaboration.

Given the pivotal role of Eimer et al.'s (2003) finding of the absence of the emotion effect without focal attention in the above-mentioned theoretical advancements, it is crucial to replicate the result by a high standard of contemporary ERP research.

text.text: Specifically, the original study lacked statistical power with a sample size of 14.

In the original study (regarding the first two aspects of findings, i.e., the emotion effects and their attentional modulation), if the emotion effect was still present without focal attention but too weak to be detected with the limited statistical power, a high-powered replication will provide additional information indispensable to the field.
Confirming (or refuting) the attentional modulation originally reported would provide a more secure foundation for debates about the automaticity of emotional face processing.

Accordingly, the current study reproduces the original experimental protocol to reassess with enhanced statistical precision the role of spatial attention in the early and late cortical dynamics of facial-expression perception.

Related to the first two aspects of Eimer et al.'s (2003) findings, there are two hypotheses: Hypothesis 1 (H1): In the emotion discrimination task (attention directed to faces), emotional faces will elicit enhanced ERPs relative to neutral faces, including: H2: In the line discrimination task (attention directed away from faces), no emotion effect as in H1 will be found in any of these five ERP activities (correspondingly H2.1 to H2.5).

text.text: Specifically, the frontal positivity between 160 and 215 ms may correspond to the vertex positive potential (VPP), an ERP component sharing a neural generator with N170 and likewise indexing early face perception (Joyce & Rossion, 2005).

text.text: The presence of an emotion effect and its attentional modulation in this window raises the possibility that N170 could exhibit similar effects when statistical power is sufficient.
Therefore, it is desirable to replicate the negative result in N170 of the Eimer et al. (2003) study (i.e., no emotion effect).

text.text: Furthermore, to go beyond only showing consistency with the original finding (if we are to obtain a non-significant result), we will also run Bayesian analysis to obtain evidence for equivalence between the emotional and neutral faces as a firm replication of the original result.
Another potential factor contributing to the absence of emotion effect in N170 is the averaged-earlobes reference used by Eimer et al. (2003).

text.text: This reference has been shown to reduce the amplitude of N170 and enhance the amplitude of VPP (Joyce & Rossion, 2005).

text.text: As such, it is possible that N170 may be able to show the emotion effect with a reference more suitable for N170.
In the literature, the common average reference is usually preferred for a strong N170 (e.g., Joyce & Rossion, 2005).

text.text: However, in the current multi-lab research, we cannot guarantee having the same electrode layout across replicating labs, rendering the common average reference undesirable because of incomparable references across labs (see Dien, 1998).

text.text: A more favourable choice is the reference electrode standardization technique (REST), which mathematically calculates a reference point at infinity where the electrical potential is zero (Yao, 2001).

text.text: Working optimally from 16 to 128 electrode positions (higher electrode density leading to better REST accuracy; Liu et al., 2015), the REST referencing produces a reliable and strong N170 component similar to that with the common average reference (Wang et al., 2019), and importantly, does not vary with the electrode layout.

text.text: Therefore, in addition to the replication pipeline with a reference same as or similar to that used in Eimer et al. (2003), we will run another pre-processing pipeline employing the REST reference for the analysis of N170 and the early frontal positivity (potentially similar to VPP).

text.text: Following the above discussion, in the present replication, we will reassess whether N170 responds differently to emotional and neutral faces.
The original findings of Eimer et al. (2003) lead to the third hypothesis:
text.formatted: The original findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref> lead to the third hypothesis:

text.text: H3: N170 will show no emotion effect (i.e., no differences between emotional and neutral faces), regardless of the attentional manipulation.
This will be complemented by evidence for equivalence from Bayesian analysis.
The final aspect of Eimer et al.'s (2003) findings is the absence of any difference in the ERPs among the six basic emotions.
text.formatted: The final aspect of <ref type="bibr">Eimer et al.'s (2003)</ref> findings is the absence of any difference in the ERPs among the six basic emotions.

text.text: This finding suggested that all emotions are processed in essentially the same way.
Subsequent research, however, has shown that different emotions can be processed differently.

Negatively valenced and potentially threatening expressions (e.g., fear and anger) tend to be more salient and are processed more rapidly and automatically than other emotions, a pattern known as the negativity bias (Ito et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2003). Luo et al. (2010) confirmed this bias, demonstrating that negative expressions, particularly fear, elicit an enhanced P1 component even when attention is not focused on the faces.

(2010)</ref> confirmed this bias, demonstrating that negative expressions, particularly fear, elicit an enhanced P1 component even when attention is not focused on the faces.

text.text: Threatening faces likewise produce attentionindependent enhancements of the EPN relative to neutral or friendly faces (Aguado et al., 2019; Rellecke et al., 2011; Schupp et al., 2004 Schupp et al., , 2006;; Weidner et al., 2022).

text.text: Some of these studies employed emotion categorization tasks similar to that in the Eimer et al. (2003) study (Ito et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2003).

text.text: Meanwhile, others either demanded more than categorizing emotional and neutral faces and requested participants to identify facial expressions (Aguado et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2010; Weidner et al., 2022), or reduced the attentional engagement by studying facial expression processing in passive viewing conditions (Rellecke et al., 2011; Schupp et al., 2004).

text.text: Therefore, it is unlikely that the differences in the findings could be explained by task differences.
These observations motivated us to explore whether ERPs would differ across the six emotions in the current replication.
Following the results of Eimer et al. (2003), we will test the final hypothesis:
text.formatted: Following the results of <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref>, we will test the final hypothesis:

text.text: H4: ERPs do not differ across the six basic emotions in any of the measurements stated in H1 or N170, regardless of the attentional manipulation.
This will be complemented by evidence for equivalence from Bayesian analysis.

To test these hypotheses, EEG data will be acquired in each replicating lab using the same stimuli and experimental procedure as those in the original study, along with the recording parameters staying as close as possible.

Individual datasets from the replicating labs will be separately analysed by the leading lab using the same analysis pipelines, then put into internal random-effects meta-analyses for pooled estimates with higher statistical power.

The original study's key results were several significant Task × Emotion interactions ("Task × Valence interactions" in the original publication's wording) that demonstrated enhanced ERP responses to emotional faces relative to neutral faces when focal attention was allocated to the faces (emotion task), but not when attention was directed towards line segments (line task) (Eimer et al., 2003; sample size N = 14).
text.formatted: The original study's key results were several significant Task × Emotion interactions ("Task × Valence interactions" in the original publication's wording) that demonstrated enhanced ERP responses to emotional faces relative to neutral faces when focal attention was allocated to the faces (emotion task), but not when attention was directed towards line segments (line task) <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Eimer et al., 2003</ref>; sample size N = 14).

text.text: This attention-dependent emotion effect was observed in five ERP activities over four temporal phases, including an early frontal positivity (160-215 ms, F(1,13) = 5.2, p < .05), a frontocentral positivity and an occipitotemporal negativity (both at 220-315 ms, Fs > 7.2, ps < .02), and positivities over frontal, central and parietal regions (320-495 and 500-700 ms, Fs > 10.0, ps < .01).
text.formatted: This attention-dependent emotion effect was observed in five ERP activities over four temporal phases, including an early frontal positivity (160-215 ms, F(1,13) = 5.2, p < .05), a frontocentral positivity and an occipitotemporal negativity (both at 220-315 ms, Fs > 7.2, ps < .02), and positivities over frontal, central and parietal regions (320-495 and 500-700 ms, Fs > 10.0, ps < .01).

text.text: Following the #EEGManyLabs recommendations (Pavlov et al., 2021) and recognizing that ERP studies often overestimate effect sizes due to small samples (Clayson et al., 2019), we calculated the required sample size of the replication.
text.formatted: Following the #EEGManyLabs recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Pavlov et al., 2021)</ref> and recognizing that ERP studies often overestimate effect sizes due to small samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Clayson et al., 2019)</ref>, we calculated the required sample size of the replication.

text.text: The calculation was based on the weakest original significant Task x Emotion interaction found in 160-215 ms (F = 5.2, corresponding to η² p = 0.2857).
We targeted 90% power to detect an effect half of the original effect (i.e., η² p = 0.1429) at an alpha level of .02.
With these settings, an a priori power analysis using MorePower 6.0.4 (Campbell & Thompson, 2012) indicated a sample size of 82.
text.formatted: With these settings, an a priori power analysis using MorePower 6.0.4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Campbell & Thompson, 2012)</ref> indicated a sample size of 82.

text.text: However, this sample size puts up a high demand on each lab's data collection work and is potentially impractical.

Therefore, we have decided to reduce the required sample size from each replicating lab to 41 (half of the initial estimation; this reduced sample size is not related to the number or replicating labs).

Following the meta-analytic theory (e.g., Borenstein et al., 2021), with a fixed total sample size, distributing participants across sites and then meta-analysing their effect sizes yields the same point estimate and nearly identical precision, provided the between-site heterogeneity is accounted for (see also Paul et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Following the meta-analytic theory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Borenstein et al., 2021)</ref>, with a fixed total sample size, distributing participants across sites and then meta-analysing their effect sizes yields the same point estimate and nearly identical precision, provided the between-site heterogeneity is accounted for (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Paul et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As such, reducing the per-lab sample from 82 to 41 will not compromise the meta-analytic power of the study as long as the overall sample is large enough.
Each replicating lab will collect behavioural and EEG data from 41 participants.
If any participants are to be excluded from the analysis, more participants will be tested to replace the excluded participants to obtain usable data from 41 participants in each replicating lab.

Following the decision to reduce the sample size per replicating lab from 82 to 41, we did a sensitivity power analysis using MorePower 6.0.4 to assess the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) that each replicating lab can achieve for the Task x Emotion interactions.
With 90% power and an alpha level of .02, the analysis showed an MDES of η² p = 0.2587.
This effect size is smaller than that of the weakest significant Task x Emotion interaction in the original study (frontal positivity at 160-215 ms, η² p = 0.2857).

Expressed as power, each replicating lab will have 94.3% power to detect an effect of the magnitude reported for the weakest original interaction, and 98.9% and 99.9% power for the effects reported in the 220-315 ms and the later time windows.
By comparison, the original study, with N = 14 and an alpha level of .05, could only reliably detect effects of η² p = 0.468 or larger at 90% power.
Therefore, even with the halved sample size, each replicating lab is about twice as sensitive as the study being replicated, and at a more stringent alpha level.
Furthermore, the metaanalysis will be highly powered.
The replication study has eight participating labs so far, giving a total sample size of 328.

With this pooled sample size, at 90% power and alpha level of .02, we will be able to detect the effect as small as η² p = 0.0386 (a small effect size). Eimer et al. (2003) did not find any difference in the N170 component, neither did they observe any differences across the six basic emotions.

(2003)</ref> did not find any difference in the N170 component, neither did they observe any differences across the six basic emotions.

text.text: The current replication plans to further explore these patterns by including negative hypotheses (H3 and H4) based on the original study.

To check whether the replication study will have enough power to statistically assess weak effects and be able to avoid mistakenly drawing negative conclusions, we ran further sensitivity power analyses with the same power and alpha level settings.
For the emotion effect in N170 and its interaction with task (H3), same as the frontal positivity above, the MDES is η² p = 0.0386 (a small effect size).
For the facial expression effect and its interaction with the other factors (H4), the MDES is η² p = 0.0120 (a small effect size).
Therefore, the planned analysis is capable of reliably detecting small effect sizes and will only show null findings if the effects are below these levels.

At the time of the Registered Report Stage 1 manuscript, apart from the leading lab in the UK, seven labs from seven countries (Australia, China, France, Spain, Türkiye, UK, and USA) have joined the project, equipped with EEG systems from four EEG equipment manufacturers (ANT Neuro, BioSemi, BrainProducts, and Neuroscan).

As such, various aspects of EEG data acquisition will differ, including but not limited to EEG system make and model, electrode design (e.g., active vs. passive), electrode layout, electric conducting medium (conductive gel, saline, or direct electrode contact without medium), baseline electric noise level, recording software, trigger port (e.g., parallel port, USB port, lab streaming layer), trigger latency accuracy, laboratory layout (related to participant experience), working language, researcher ethnicity, participant ethnicity, and working habit/style of researchers.
To minimize unnecessary variations, the data acquisition procedure is pre-determined and to be followed precisely by each replicating lab.
Before a replicating lab starts collecting data, we will also ensure the timing accuracy of event triggers.

If necessary, we will use the open-source stimulus-latency instrument developed by #EEGManyLabs (ElectroTime; Van den Bosch et al., 2026; see also https://electrotime.org/) to confirm the trigger latency.

We will evaluate whether these differences influence replicability with the internal random-effects meta-analysis, which allows cross-dataset heterogeneity to be assessed.

text.text: Volunteers are eligible for the study if they are 1) aged 18-60 years, 2) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, 3) self-reporting to have no neurological condition, and 4) without any skin allergies.

Each replicating lab will record participants' age, handedness (left, right, ambidextrous), total years of education (the total number of years in formal schooling starting from elementary school), highest level of education, and length of time spent in the country (all self-reported).
We will record further demographic information of each participant, including their identified gender, ethnic origin, and identified race.

The demographic questionnaire (Appendix 1) is adapted from the recommendation of Joint Commitment for Action on Inclusion and Diversity in Publishing for its well-known capability to capture inclusivity and diversity (Royal Society of Chemistry, 2020).
The answer option "prefer not to disclose" is removed from the ethnic origin and identified race questions due to their importance in the exploratory LMM analysis.
Participants will have to withdraw from the study if they do not want to disclose information about their ethnic origin or race.
Gender information will also be collected using this document, with the "prefer not to disclose" kept as an answer option.

All faces were in greyscale against a black background with external features removed.
In the current replication, we will use the same 70 images.
Provided by the lab of the original study, these are 8-bit greyscale bitmap images (100×142 pixels, portrait layout).
To be authentic to the original stimuli, these images will be used in the replication despite the relatively low image resolution.
Viewing distance in each replicating lab is determined to ensure the face images will extend the visual angles as reported in the original study.
To avoid clearly noticeable quality degradation, we will use the images in their original display size if possible.
If using the original image size requires a viewing distance less than 50 cm or is not allowed by the lab setup, we will stretch to enlarge the images but only up to 150% of the original size.

text.text: All replicating labs will make necessary changes to the program, including translating or rewording of the instructions for their participants, changing the method of manual responses, changing the trigger port address, changing the trigger values for block start and end, and slight tweaking for their own PsychoPy version.
As stated above, each lab will try to stay with a 100% scaling factor if the hardware and lab setup allow.
All replicating labs' experiment programs will also be available on the repository.
The experiment has 24 blocks, each of which has 80 trials.
Participants will complete two discrimination tasks (emotion and line tasks), each comprising 12 consecutive blocks, with the task order counterbalanced across participants.
Throughout the experiment, participants will be instructed to keep their eye gaze on the fixation cross and to minimize eye blinks and eye movements.
In each block, no matter what the task is, neutral face pairs randomly appear on half of the trials, with emotional face pairs randomly appearing on the other half.

Each of the six facial expressions (angry, disgusted, fearful, happy, sad, surprised; i.e. six block types) is presented on the emotional face trials for two blocks, with the order of block types randomized across participants.
The length of each line segment in the display varies independently (short and long lines are equally likely to appear on either side of the display).
Each trial presents the stimulus display for 300 ms, followed by a 2,000-ms interval before the next trial starts (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Each trial presents the stimulus display for 300 ms, followed by a 2,000-ms interval before the next trial starts (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In the emotion task, participants will be asked to discriminate between emotional and neutral face pairs and ignore the line segments, and to respond as quickly and accurately as possible with left-or right-hand keypresses ('z' or 'm') for neutral or emotional faces.
In the line task, participants will determine whether the line segments are identical or different in length while ignoring the faces, and to respond quickly and accurately by pressing 'z' or 'm'.
The response-hand mapping is counterbalanced between tasks and across participants.
Manual responses made within 2,000 ms from the stimulus onset will be accepted.
The trial sequence will run regardless of the presence or timing of manual responses.
After each block, feedback on participant performance (mean accuracy and RT) will be provided on the screen.

Methodologically, randomizing inter-trial intervals (i.e., interval jitter) is widely adopted in ERP research to remove electric activities evoked by preceding trials from the ERP responses of the current trial (Luck, 2014). Eimer et al. (2003) did not employ this and instead used a single and long interval duration (2,000 ms).
text.formatted: Methodologically, randomizing inter-trial intervals (i.e., interval jitter) is widely adopted in ERP research to remove electric activities evoked by preceding trials from the ERP responses of the current trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Luck, 2014)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref> did not employ this and instead used a single and long interval duration (2,000 ms).

text.text: In the original study, the ERPs during the pre-stimulus baseline period were sufficiently flat, suggesting that the absence of interval jitter was not a technical concern.

Furthermore, despite the use of a fixed interval between trials, anticipatory manual responses are not to be expected because of the use of forced-choice responses instead of simple reactions (hence the ERP results are not expected to be influenced).

Additionally, another potential issue is that participants may develop temporal expectations regarding the onsets of forthcoming stimuli, and as a result lead to some preparatory brain activities (e.g., Pütz et al., 2025).

(2003) study, despite this possibility, we will apply a verbatim adoption of the original trial sequence to avoid any potential difficulties of interpreting results if we obtain any findings different from those of the original study.

text.text: Before running the experimental blocks, each participant will go through a practice block for each task.

Participants will stop practising and proceed to the experimental blocks if they have reached 80% accuracy in a practice block in each task, as in the original study (M. Eimer, personal communication, 31 July 2025), with the accuracy calculated as the ratio of the number of correctly responded trials to the number of total trials (i.e., trials with no responses are treated as incorrect trials).
If a participant does not reach the 80% accuracy level after one practice block, up to two more practice blocks will be carried out.
If a participant's mean accuracy in a practice block remains below 80% after three practice blocks for any task, this participant will not proceed to the experimental blocks.
