text.text: Table 2 summarizes the EEG data acquisition, pre-processing, and measurement pipelines.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> summarizes the EEG data acquisition, pre-processing, and measurement pipelines.

text.text: All data will be acquired with the specified filter and sampling rate settings.

Each lab can have a different number of electrodes, but must be able to record from these key locations: frontal pole (Fpz; Fp1 instead if Fpz is not possible), frontal (F3, Fz, F4), central (C3, Cz, C4), parietal (P3, Pz, P4), lateral temporal (P7, P8), and lateral occipital (PO7, PO8), horizontal electrooculograph (HEOG; either as a single bipolar channel or as two monopolar channels, with the electrodes placed at the outer canthi or two lateral peri-auricular sites as close as possible to the outer canthi), and two separate earlobes (if earlobes are not possible, separate mastoids, otherwise TP9/TP10 or T9/T10 instead).

To maximize the accuracy of the independent component analysis (ICA) and the REST re-referencing, each lab is encouraged to record EEG from as many channels as possible (see the "advanced pipeline" subsection below).
The collected data will be transferred to the leading lab for data preprocessing and statistical analysis using the same steps, strictly following the pre-registered pipelines.
The raw anonymized data will also be shared on G-Node (https://gin.g-node.org/EEGManyLabs) following the BIDS standard.
text.formatted: The raw anonymized data will also be shared on G-Node (<ref type="url" target="https://gin.g-node.org/EEGManyLabs">https://gin.g- node.org/EEGManyLabs</ref>) following the BIDS standard.

text.text: [insert Table 2 here] In Table 2, next to the pipeline employed in the original study (Eimer et al., 2003), three pipelines are listed.
text.formatted: [insert Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2 here]</ref> In Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>, next to the pipeline employed in the original study <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Eimer et al., 2003)</ref>, three pipelines are listed.

text.text: First, there is the "replication pipeline" in which we stay as close as possible to the protocol of the original study.
The second pipeline ("advanced pipeline") is a revised pipeline informed by the current EEG research practice.
The last pipeline ("REST pipeline") employs the REST re-referencing process for the N170 and early frontal positivity analysis.
The EEG data acquisition steps remain the same in all three pipelines.

Despite that Eimer et al. (2003) mentioned linked-earlobe reference for data acquisition, the original study in fact used the left earlobe as the online reference, and later digitally re-referenced the recordings to the averaged earlobes (M. Eimer, personal communication, 16 September 2025).
text.formatted: Despite that <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref> mentioned linked-earlobe reference for data acquisition, the original study in fact used the left earlobe as the online reference, and later digitally re-referenced the recordings to the averaged earlobes (M. <ref type="bibr">Eimer, personal communication, 16 September 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In EEG research, linked-earlobe referencing is not advisable due to the current shunting problem (e.g., Ollikainen et al., 2000).
text.formatted: In EEG research, linked-earlobe referencing is not advisable due to the current shunting problem (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Ollikainen et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: With physically linked electrodes, an electric current between the two electrodes can occur.
This can distort the EEG recordings and reduce hemispheric differences in the results (Luck, 2014; Nunez & Srinivasan, 2006; Regan, 1989).
text.formatted: This can distort the EEG recordings and reduce hemispheric differences in the results <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Luck, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Nunez & Srinivasan, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Regan, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, as in the original study, the replication will use a single-electrode online reference.

As the physical reference is a built-in and noncustomizable component in some EEG systems, each replicating lab can determine their own online reference, with the single-earlobe or single-mastoid option preferred if possible.
In the ANT Neuro Waveguard Nets, the physical reference is linked Cz and CPz.

To avoid the current shunting problem and also allow the online reference location to be regained for data analysis after the re-referencing process, only one electrode (Cz or CPz) will be used for the online reference.
This will be achieved by removing the sponge tip at the other reference electrode position.

To be consistent with the original study, data from both earlobes or mastoids need to be obtained (as either an online reference or a monopolar channel), so that they can be used for offline re-referencing.
If a replicating lab cannot apply earlobe or mastoid electrodes, TP9/TP10 or T9/T10 will be used in place of earlobes (Clayson et al., 2021; Jovanović et al., 2025).
text.formatted: If a replicating lab cannot apply earlobe or mastoid electrodes, TP9/TP10 or T9/T10 will be used in place of earlobes <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clayson et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Jovanović et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Two settings are changed from the original study.
First, Eimer et al. (2003) used an online bandpass filter of 0.1-40 Hz.
text.formatted: First, <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref> used an online bandpass filter of 0.1-40 Hz.

text.text: To avoid unnecessarily removing data and to keep as much as possible in the replication study, no online filter will be applied unless a replicating lab's EEG system does not have the capability of DC recording.
In this case, a 0.1 Hz highpass filter will be applied.

The 0.1-40 Hz bandpass filtering will be achieved offline with a digital filter (i.e., 0.1-40 Hz bandpass filter if no online filter is used; 40 Hz lowpass filter if a 0.1 Hz online highpass filter is used).
Second, a higher sampling rate (500 or 512 Hz, as seen fit for each individual EEG system) will be used (200 Hz in the original study) to provide a higher temporal resolution.

All EEG data will be imported into EEGLAB (Delorme & Makeig, 2004) using data importation plugins and processed using two pipelines (Table 2), i.e., a direct replication pipeline that follows the original study as closely as possible, and an advanced pipeline following more recent standards.
text.formatted: All EEG data will be imported into EEGLAB <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Delorme & Makeig, 2004)</ref> using data importation plugins and processed using two pipelines (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>), i.e., a direct replication pipeline that follows the original study as closely as possible, and an advanced pipeline following more recent standards.

text.text: The pre-processing codes for both pipelines are available online (https://osf.io/4n2t8/).
text.formatted: The pre-processing codes for both pipelines are available online (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/4n2t8/">https://osf.io/4n2t8/</ref>).

text.text: These codes have been tested with pilot data collected from several replicating labs for quality assurance and the choice of pre-processing parameters.

The data will be re-referenced to the average voltage of earlobes (or averaged mastoids, or averaged TP9/TP10, or averaged T9/T10 if EEG data from earlobes are unavailable) before being down-sampled to 200 Hz (the same as in the original study).
A bipolar HEOG channel will be generated if HEOG data were acquired as separate monopolar channels.
A digital bandpass filter of 0.1-40 Hz will then be applied.
The filtered data will be segmented into epochs ranging from 100 ms before to 700 ms after stimulus onset, then baseline corrected for the 100-ms pre-onset period.

Afterwards, artefact rejection will be carried out to remove epochs contaminated by horizontal eye movements (exceeding ±30 µV at the HEOG channel), eye blinks (exceeding ±60 µV at Fpz or Fp1 if Fpz is unavailable), and other artefacts (exceeding ±80 µV at any other key electrodes, including F3, Fz, F4, C3, Cz, C4, P7, P3, Pz, P4, P8, PO7, and PO8).
If more than 50% of epochs in any of the two tasks from a participant are to be removed by this step, this particular participant will be removed from any further analysis.
We will apply the 50% threshold to each task separately, because the block design of the two tasks may lead to poor quality data in one task only, disproportionately affecting results from one task.
Finally, accepted epochs carrying correct responses will be averaged to create ERP waveforms for each condition (i.e., each of the 24 task, block type, and emotion combinations).
For ERP quantification, we will use the same channels and time windows reported in Eimer et al. (2003) for all the ERP activities.
text.formatted: For ERP quantification, we will use the same channels and time windows reported in <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref> for all the ERP activities.

text.text: Specifically, N170 will be quantified as mean amplitude at P7 and P8 (labelled T5 and T6 in the original study) over the time window of 160-200 ms.

Five successive time windows will then be used to quantify mean ERP amplitudes over five scalp regions separately, namely frontal (F3, Fz, F4), central (C3, Cz, C4), parietal (P3, Pz, P4), temporal (P7, P8), and lateral occipital (PO7 and PO8; labelled OL and OR in the original study) channels.

These time windows are 120-155, 160-215, 220-315, 320-495, and 500-800 ms, which cover the periods showing emotional expression differences in studies predating the original study (Eimer & Holmes, 2002; Holmes et al., 2003).
text.formatted: These time windows are 120-155, 160-215, 220-315, 320-495, and 500-800 ms, which cover the periods showing emotional expression differences in studies predating the original study <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Eimer & Holmes, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Holmes et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: The data will be re-referenced and digitally filtered as above, but not be down-sampled.
Afterwards, we will apply the ICA method (Onton et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Afterwards, we will apply the ICA method <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Onton et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: For this purpose, we will create a copy of the dataset and highpass filter it at 2 Hz (Klug & Gramann, 2021).
text.formatted: For this purpose, we will create a copy of the dataset and highpass filter it at 2 Hz <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Klug & Gramann, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Then, any data with no event triggers for longer than 5,000 ms will be removed.
Independent component (IC) weights will then be computed with the Adaptive Mixture ICA (AMICA) method (Palmer et al., 2012), and be transferred to the original data.
text.formatted: Independent component (IC) weights will then be computed with the Adaptive Mixture ICA (AMICA) method <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Palmer et al., 2012)</ref>, and be transferred to the original data.

text.text: Another data copy will be created with the 2-Hz highpass filter for IC classification, which will employ ICLabel (Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019) to automatically identify IC sources.
text.formatted: Another data copy will be created with the 2-Hz highpass filter for IC classification, which will employ ICLabel <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019)</ref> to automatically identify IC sources.

text.text: ICs identified as eye, muscle, heart, line noise, and channel noise with more than 80% probability will be flagged for rejection.
These flagged ICs will be removed from the original dataset.
After the ICA procedure, the dataset will be segmented into 800-ms epochs (-100 to 700 ms relative to stimulus onset), baseline corrected, and artefact rejected.

For artefact rejection, in addition to the three criteria above (eye movements, blinks, strong artefacts), trials showing prolonged weak activity (absolute voltage below 0.5 µV for more than 200 ms) at any of the key electrode locations (F3, Fz, F4, C3, Cz, C4, P7, P3, Pz, P4, P8, PO7, PO8) will also be rejected.
As in the replication pipeline, a 50% epoch rejection threshold for each task will be used for participant removal.
Average ERP waveforms will then be created based on epochs with correct behavioural responses.
ERP waveforms will be quantified at the same selection of channels as in Eimer et al. (2003) except for the N170 component.
text.formatted: ERP waveforms will be quantified at the same selection of channels as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref> except for the N170 component.

text.text: In the original study, N170 was quantified at P7/P8.
In the research of face processing, both electrode pairs P7/P8 and PO7/PO8 are usually involved with N170 amplitude measurement (for summaries, see Morgan et al., 2008; Rossion & Jacques, 2008).
text.formatted: In the research of face processing, both electrode pairs P7/P8 and PO7/PO8 are usually involved with N170 amplitude measurement (for summaries, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Morgan et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Rossion & Jacques, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Despite that N170 is often illustrated at PO7/PO8 in the literature (e.g., Itier et al., 2007; Rossion & Jacques, 2011), interestingly, when being measured on its own (i.e., not measured as peak-to-peak difference from P1; e.g., Tanaka, 2018), N170 typically shows maximal amplitudes at P7/P8 instead of PO7/PO8 (e.g., Eimer, 2011; Gao et al., 2019; Itier et al., 2007; Itier & Taylor, 2004; Kuefner et al., 2010; Prieto et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Despite that N170 is often illustrated at PO7/PO8 in the literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Itier et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Rossion & Jacques, 2011)</ref>, interestingly, when being measured on its own (i.e., not measured as peak-to-peak difference from P1; e.g., Tanaka, 2018), N170 typically shows maximal amplitudes at P7/P8 instead of PO7/PO8 (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Eimer, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Gao et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Itier et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Itier & Taylor, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Kuefner et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Prieto et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Sometimes, very strong (or even maximal) N170 amplitudes were also observed at PO9/PO10 (e.g., Gao et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2015; Rossion & Jacques, 2008).
text.formatted: Sometimes, very strong (or even maximal) N170 amplitudes were also observed at PO9/PO10 (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Gao et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Lin et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Rossion & Jacques, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In publications more recent than Eimer et al. (2003), the most common practice has been combining P7/P8 and PO7/PO8 for N170 amplitude measurement (e.g., Kuefner et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2016; Morgan et al., 2008; Rossion & Jacques, 2008; Tanaka & Jiang, 2024).
text.formatted: In publications more recent than <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref>, the most common practice has been combining P7/P8 and PO7/PO8 for N170 amplitude measurement (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Kuefner et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Liu et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Morgan et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Rossion & Jacques, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">Tanaka & Jiang, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the current replication, both electrode pairs P7/P8 and PO7/PO8 are required for data collection therefore available for data analysis.
Therefore, for better result stability, in the advanced pipeline, we will measure the average N170 amplitudes over these four locations (P7/P8 and PO7/PO8).
For the other five ERP activities, the channels for ERP quantification will remain the same as in Eimer et al. (2003), i.e., F3/Fz/F4, C3/Cz/C4, P3/Pz/P4, P7/P8, and PO7/PO8.
text.formatted: For the other five ERP activities, the channels for ERP quantification will remain the same as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref>, i.e., F3/Fz/F4, C3/Cz/C4, P3/Pz/P4, P7/P8, and PO7/PO8.

text.text: To determine the analysis windows reliably and objectively, the collapsed localizer method (Luck & Gaspelin, 2017) will be implemented separately for each replicating lab's dataset.
text.formatted: To determine the analysis windows reliably and objectively, the collapsed localizer method <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Luck & Gaspelin, 2017)</ref> will be implemented separately for each replicating lab's dataset.

text.text: From each lab's dataset, a localizer waveform will be generated for each electrode cluster (e.g., F3/Fz/F4) by averaging over these electrodes in the group, and across all conditions and participants.
Then, for each localizer waveform, the local peak amplitude (the strongest voltage) will be determined within the corresponding analysis window in the original study.
For instance, the N170 peak amplitude will be measured between 160 and 200 ms in the localizer waveform averaged over P7/P8/PO7/PO8 across all conditions and participants.

Following this protocol, the other five peak-searching windows will be 120-155, 160-215, 220-315, 320-495, and 500-800 ms (identical to the analysis windows in Eimer et al., 2003), each of which will be applied to the five electrode clusters separately (F3/Fz/F4, C3/Cz/C4, P3/Pz/P4, P7/P8/PO7/PO8, and PO7/PO8).
text.formatted: Following this protocol, the other five peak-searching windows will be 120-155, 160-215, 220-315, 320-495, and 500-800 ms (identical to the analysis windows in <ref type="bibr">Eimer et al., 2003)</ref>, each of which will be applied to the five electrode clusters separately (F3/Fz/F4, C3/Cz/C4, P3/Pz/P4, P7/P8/PO7/PO8, and PO7/PO8).

text.text: For each ERP activity, once the peak amplitude has been determined in the collapsed localizer waveform from each replicating lab, the boundaries of the meanamplitude-measurement time window will be set at 50% of the peak amplitude (scanning from the peak to the left and right of the waveform).
Our approach is a variation of the fractional peak latency procedure used for ERP latency quantification.

The fractional peak latency procedure takes the time point where an ERP waveform reaches a certain fraction (e.g., 50%) of the peak amplitude of a component as the onset of that ERP component (Kiesel et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The fractional peak latency procedure takes the time point where an ERP waveform reaches a certain fraction (e.g., 50%) of the peak amplitude of a component as the onset of that ERP component <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Kiesel et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: This method has been widely and successfully employed in the literature (e.g., Grubert & Eimer, 2023; Kompatsiari et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This method has been widely and successfully employed in the literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Grubert & Eimer, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Kompatsiari et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">Wang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Our approach adapted this method to locate the two 50%-peak-amplitude points (respectively in the ascending and descending flanks of an ERP component) to determine the mean amplitude measurement window.

Given that the averaged-mastoid reference may not be ideal for the amplitude measurement of N170 and early frontal positivity (potentially related to the VPP component), we will run an additional pre-processing pipeline employing a better re-referencing process, namely the REST method (Yao, 2001; for the MATLAB plugin, see Dong et al., 2017) to replace the averaged-mastoid re-referencing.
text.formatted: Given that the averaged-mastoid reference may not be ideal for the amplitude measurement of N170 and early frontal positivity (potentially related to the VPP component), we will run an additional pre-processing pipeline employing a better re-referencing process, namely the REST method <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">(Yao, 2001</ref>; for the MATLAB plugin, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Dong et al., 2017)</ref> to replace the averaged-mastoid re-referencing.

text.text: All other aspects will remain exactly the same as those of the advanced pipeline.
Following this pipeline, only the mean amplitudes of N170 and early frontal positivity will be analysed.
We will first check the overall accuracy of all participants.

Following the criterion used in the practice blocks, any participants showing an accuracy level lower than 80% (the ratio of the number of correctly responded trials to the number of total trials, with trials without responses being treated as incorrect trials) in any of the two tasks will be excluded from further analysis.

Given the within-subjects design, the behavioural and ERP data will be statistically assessed with repeated-measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs; with Holm correction applied to all post hoc comparisons) and paired t-tests.
The Greenhouse-Geisser correction will be applied to the ANOVAs whenever the sphericity assumption is violated.
Outputs with p values smaller than .02 will be accepted as rejection of the null hypotheses.

All analyses will be complemented by Bayesian counterparts, namely Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVAs and Bayesian paired t-tests, using the default Cauchy prior distribution, a heavytailed probability distribution which is often used as the default prior distribution for Bayesian analyses as it is suggested to be the simplest option satisfying consistency requirements for hypothesis testing (Jeffreys, 1961; Wetzels et al., 2012).
text.formatted: All analyses will be complemented by Bayesian counterparts, namely Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVAs and Bayesian paired t-tests, using the default Cauchy prior distribution, a heavytailed probability distribution which is often used as the default prior distribution for Bayesian analyses as it is suggested to be the simplest option satisfying consistency requirements for hypothesis testing <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Jeffreys, 1961;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Wetzels et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For the Bayesian t-tests, the prior on the standardized effect size δ under the alternative hypothesis is a Cauchy distribution centred on zero with the scale parameter r, that is, δ ~ Cauchy(0,r); under the null hypothesis, δ = 0.
The scale parameter (known as prior width in JASP; Love et al., 2019) is set to r = 0.707 for all fixed effects, except otherwise specified for H3 (the emotion effect in N170).
text.formatted: The scale parameter (known as prior width in JASP; <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Love et al., 2019)</ref> is set to r = 0.707 for all fixed effects, except otherwise specified for H3 (the emotion effect in N170).

text.text: For the Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVAs, we follow the default model structure of Rouder et al. (2012) as implemented in JASP (Love et al., 2019).
text.formatted: For the Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVAs, we follow the default model structure of <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Rouder et al. (2012)</ref> as implemented in JASP <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Love et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The intercept is given a uniform prior, the residual variance a Jeffreys prior p(σ 2 ) ∝ 1/σ 2 , and the standardized fixed effects are assigned the default ANOVA prior that can be expressed via a g-prior with g ~ Inverse-Gamma(1/2, r 2 /2).
This is equivalent to placing a multivariate Cauchy prior with scale r on the standardised fixed effects.
The participant random-effect prior width is set to 1, as in the JASP default, and random slopes were included for all within-subject effects except the highest-order interaction.
The Bayesian factors will be quantified by comparing across matched models.
We will descriptively interpret the Bayesian factor results using the categories summarized by Lee and Wagenmakers (2014).
text.formatted: We will descriptively interpret the Bayesian factor results using the categories summarized by <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Lee and Wagenmakers (2014)</ref>.

text.text: For the BF10 value evidencing the alternative hypothesis (the opposite of the null hypothesis), 1 means no evidence in favour of the alternative hypothesis; 1 to 3 is anecdotal evidence; 3 to 10 is moderate evidence; 10 to 30 is strong evidence; 30 to 100 is very strong evidence; above 100 is extreme evidence.
The reciprocal of BF10 (i.e., BF01) will suggest the corresponding evidence in favour of the null hypothesis.
If the frequentist and Bayesian analysis results diverge, we will favour the frequentist interpretation first as it is a direct replication of the original study.
The Bayesian results will complement the frequentist interpretation.
Differences in reaction time (RT) and accuracy between the emotion and line tasks will be first assessed using two paired t-tests.
For each task, the RT and accuracy data will then be analysed using ANOVAs and Bayesian ANOVAs as stated above.
In the emotion task, a two-way ANOVA will be conducted with within-subject factors Emotion (emotional vs. neutral) and Block Type (the six facial expressions).
For the line task, an additional factor (Line Type with two levels identical lines vs. different lines) will be included, resulting in a three-way ANOVA.
For each ERP activity resulting from each of the two pre-processing pipelines, the analysis of mean ERP amplitudes will start with a three-way ANOVA.
The three factors are Task (emotion vs. line), Emotion (emotional vs. neutral), and Block Type (the six basic facial expressions).
Following any significant main effects of Block Type in these ANOVAs, post hoc tests using Holm corrections will be used.
Consistent with the original study, planned two-way ANOVAs will be performed for each task (irrespective of the Task x Emotion interaction outcome).
Corresponding Bayesian ANOVAs will also be implemented using a Cauchy prior width of 0.707 except for H3.
For H1 and H2 (predictions of positive findings), frequentist analysis outputs with p < .02 in the same direction as in the original study will be accepted as successful replications.
text.formatted: For H1 and H2 (predictions of positive findings), frequentist analysis outputs with p < .02 in the same direction as in the original study will be accepted as successful replications.

text.text: BF10 ≥ 3 in the same direction as in the original study and BF10 ≤ 0.333 will be accepted as evidence for the alternative and null hypothesis, respectively.

For H3 and H4 (predictions of negative findings), results showing p < .02 or BF10 ≥ 3 in either direction and BF10 ≤ 0.333 will be accepted as evidence for the alternative and null hypothesis, respectively.
text.formatted: For H3 and H4 (predictions of negative findings), results showing p < .02 or BF10 ≥ 3 in either direction and BF10 ≤ 0.333 will be accepted as evidence for the alternative and null hypothesis, respectively.

text.text: Results confirming H1 and H2 should show a significant Task x Emotion interaction in the three-way ANOVA.

Planned two-way ANOVAs should demonstrate significantly higher amplitudes for the emotional than neutral faces in the emotion task (Emotion main effect) in the five ERP activities, including frontal positivity 160-215 ms (H1.1), frontocentral positivity 220-315 ms (H1.2), occipitotemporal negativity 220-315 ms (H1.3), frontal-central-parietal positivity 320-495 ms (H1.4), and frontal-central-parietal positivity 500-700 ms (H1.5).
The corresponding Emotion main effects are expected to turn out in favour of the null hypothesis in the line task (H2.1 to H2.5).
For H3, no significant Task x Emotion interaction is expected in the frequentist threeway ANOVA.
The following two-way ANOVAs should also show no main effect of Emotion in either the emotion or line task.

As in the original study, frequentist paired t-tests will be performed to compare the emotional and neutral faces in the emotion task, separately for the six basic emotions (i.e., the six Block Type levels).
No significant differences are expected to be found in these t-tests.

In the Bayesian ANOVAs for H3, we will follow the same protocol (three-way ANOVA followed by two-way ANOVAs for the two tasks separately) and take evidence for the null hypothesis as confirmation of H3.
One important change to make is that we will set several Cauchy prior widths for the emotion effect following the study of Hinojosa et al. (2015).
text.formatted: One important change to make is that we will set several Cauchy prior widths for the emotion effect following the study of <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Hinojosa et al. (2015)</ref>.

text.text: Their meta-analysis found a significantly stronger N170 in response to emotional faces than to neutral faces (with all emotions combined), displaying a mean Cohen's d of 0.3325.
Furthermore, they also found different emotion effect sizes across five emotions in their meta-analysis.

Three of the emotion effects were significant, namely angry vs. neutral (Cohen's d = 0.2062), fearful vs. neutral (0.4219), and happy vs. neutral (0.2552); and two were non-significant, namely disgusted vs. neutral (0.4217, but with a large confidence interval that included zero) and sad vs. neutral (0.0769).

Taking these results together, we observed that the plausible emotion effect in N170 is likely to be relatively small (in a range between 0.2062 and 0.4219), and that the emotion effect size is uncertain depending on the specific emotion -these probably were the reasons why Eimer et al. (2003) did not show any significant emotion effect in N170.
text.formatted: Taking these results together, we observed that the plausible emotion effect in N170 is likely to be relatively small (in a range between 0.2062 and 0.4219), and that the emotion effect size is uncertain depending on the specific emotion -these probably were the reasons why <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eimer et al. (2003)</ref> did not show any significant emotion effect in N170.

text.text: These two observations suggest that the N170 data probably will not be highly informative, so that the different prior widths can reasonably lead to different Bayes factors (Depaoli et al., 2020; Vanpaemel, 2010).
text.formatted: These two observations suggest that the N170 data probably will not be highly informative, so that the different prior widths can reasonably lead to different Bayes factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Depaoli et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Vanpaemel, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, in the Bayesian ANOVAs for H3, we will specify three Cauchy prior widths for the Emotion factor to replace the default prior width (r = 0.707), corresponding to the reported values from Hinojosa et al. (2015) (the prior widths for all the other fixed effects will be kept at the default value of 0.707).
text.formatted: Therefore, in the Bayesian ANOVAs for H3, we will specify three Cauchy prior widths for the Emotion factor to replace the default prior width (r = 0.707), corresponding to the reported values from <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Hinojosa et al. (2015)</ref> (the prior widths for all the other fixed effects will be kept at the default value of 0.707).

text.text: The three prior widths are r = 0.3325, 0.2062, and 0.4219, at which the prior median absolute effect size (i.e., the value for which P(|δ| < r) = .50) equals respectively the overall, the smallest, and the largest emotion effect reported in the meta-analysis of Hinojosa et al. (2015).
text.formatted: The three prior widths are r = 0.3325, 0.2062, and 0.4219, at which the prior median absolute effect size (i.e., the value for which P(|δ| < r) = .50) equals respectively the overall, the smallest, and the largest emotion effect reported in the meta-analysis of <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Hinojosa et al. (2015)</ref>.

text.text: This protocol reflects our expectation that the plausible effect sizes are more concentrated near zero than the default Cauchy prior width of 0.707.

The default scale parameter (prior width) of r = 0.707 assigns 65.7% of the prior probability to absolute effects larger than d = 0.4219, the largest emotion effect reported by Hinojosa et al. (2015), whereas r = 0.3325, 0.2062 and 0.4219 assign 42.5%, 28.9% and 50.0% respectively.

(2015)</ref>, whereas r = 0.3325, 0.2062 and 0.4219 assign 42.5%, 28.9% and 50.0% respectively.

text.text: For consistency, the follow-up two-way ANOVAs (for the two tasks separately) will use the same prior as in the starting three-way ANOVA, despite that Hinojosa et al. (2015) reported significantly larger effect size in the non-direct task (attention directed away from faces, Cohen's d = 0.3574) than in the direct task (attention directed to faces, d = 0.2025).
text.formatted: For consistency, the follow-up two-way ANOVAs (for the two tasks separately) will use the same prior as in the starting three-way ANOVA, despite that <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Hinojosa et al. (2015)</ref> reported significantly larger effect size in the non-direct task (attention directed away from faces, Cohen's d = 0.3574) than in the direct task (attention directed to faces, d = 0.2025).

text.text: Given that these two d values are within or very close to the range of our chosen prior widths (0.2062, 0.3325, 0.4219), we do not expect to encounter any potential issue in our protocol.

Afterwards, in the emotion task, as in the plan for the frequentist analysis, we will follow up each Bayesian ANOVA with six Bayesian paired t-tests for the six emotions, all using the same prior setting as in the preceding ANOVA.

With these three specified Cauchy prior widths (nothing else will be changed in the Bayesian ANOVAs), we will run Bayesian sensitivity analysis (not to be confused with the sensitivity power analysis) to check the robustness of the Bayesian ANOVA results for N170.
If the Bayesian evidence classification (e.g., anecdotal, moderate, strong) does not change across priors, we will conclude the Bayesian results to be robust.
Alternatively, we will report the results as prior-sensitive.
This approach will help us confidently conclude whether there is an emotion effect in N170 and the plausible effect size.
H4 is relevant to all the analyses planned above.
The absence of the Block Type difference (i.e., no differences among the six emotions) in all the frequentist and Bayesian ANOVAs described above can be considered support for H4.
However, it is important to note that, in the design of the original study, each block contains both emotional and neutral faces with equal probabilities.
The inclusion of the neutral face data (50% of the dataset) in the analysis will reduce the power to detect facial expression differences.

Hence, to directly test H4, instead of relying on the exact replication analyses mentioned above, we will run dedicated ANOVAs (both frequentists and Bayesian) with only the emotional face data to directly compare the six emotions.
This will remove the Emotion (emotional vs. neutral) factor and turn the analysis into a two-way ANOVA of Task x Emotion Type.
The factor Emotion Type has six levels corresponding to the six emotion types (we will not use the name "Block Type" anymore given that no full data from any block will be used).
Furthermore, it is difficult to directly run a meta-analysis on the effect of Emotion, which has six levels and does not have direction information.
Therefore, we will adopt a different approach for the assessment of H4.

For each of the six ERP activities (the five listed in H1 plus N170), we will run the frequentist Task x Emotion Type ANOVA (still only using the emotional face data) on the whole sample across all replicating labs, then follow up with a planned one-way ANOVA (only frequentist) for each task.
This is to check the possibility of any evidence supporting the cross-emotion differences in ERPs.
Any significant (p < .02) one-way ANOVAs will be accepted as indications of potential ERP differences among the emotions.
text.formatted: Any significant (p < .02) one-way ANOVAs will be accepted as indications of potential ERP differences among the emotions.

text.text: We will then analyse individual replicating labs' data (emotional trials only) with paired t-tests (both frequentist and Bayesian) contrasting all emotion pair combinations.
The Bayesian prior width will be set to 0.707.
To evaluate the replication success of the original study, meta-analyses of ERP data will be carried out following the #EEGManyLabs protocol (Pavlov et al., 2021).
text.formatted: To evaluate the replication success of the original study, meta-analyses of ERP data will be carried out following the #EEGManyLabs protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Pavlov et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, we will run meta-analyses for the ERP data directly corresponding to the hypotheses, and will not run meta-analyses for behaviour data or any other ERP data.
Table 3 summarizes the individual analysis results that will be entered into the meta-analyses.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">3</ref> summarizes the individual analysis results that will be entered into the meta-analyses.

text.text: The frequentist analysis results will be entered into frequentist meta-analyses, whereas the Bayesian analysis results will be put into Bayesian meta-analyses.
In cases where the frequentist and Bayesian analyses diverge, we will prioritize the frequentist interpretation complemented by the Bayesian results as evidence for or against the effect.

text.text: From the frequentist analysis results in each replicating lab's dataset, effect size (Cohen's d) and its standard error (SE) will be calculated for each hypothesis and put into a random-effects meta-analysis using the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) method, with the random effect being the replicating labs.
This approach will address the heterogeneity in the datasets (due to differences in EEG systems, research practice, ethnicity/race, cultural influence, language being used, and samples).

For each positive hypothesis, the replication will be accepted as successful if the meta-analytic estimate across all replicating labs is significant (p < .02) and in the hypothesized effect direction.
text.formatted: For each positive hypothesis, the replication will be accepted as successful if the meta-analytic estimate across all replicating labs is significant (p < .02) and in the hypothesized effect direction.

text.text: For each negative hypothesis, we define successful replication as a non-significant meta-analytic estimate (p > .02).
text.formatted: For each negative hypothesis, we define successful replication as a non-significant meta-analytic estimate (p > .02).

text.text: The values to be reported include point estimate, distribution of the weighted effect sizes, 98% confidence intervals, and heterogeneity (τ² ).
For the Bayesian meta-analyses of replication results, we will extract standardized effect sizes (Cohen's d) and their associated uncertainty (credible intervals) from each individual dataset.
These will be entered into a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis to estimate the pooled effect size and between-study heterogeneity.

For each meta-analysis, we will specify a normal prior centered at 0 with SD = 0.5 on the overall effect and a weakly informative prior on the heterogeneity parameter (half-Cauchy with a scale of 0.5).

Replication success for positive findings will be evaluated by examining whether the pooled posterior distribution supports an effect in the predicted direction and whether the Bayes Factor in favor of the alternative hypothesis (BF₁₀) exceeds 3, which is consistent with moderate-to-strong evidence.
Replication success for negative findings (null hypotheses) will be demonstrated by BF10 ≤ 0.333.
This approach will allow us to quantify the cumulative evidence across replication datasets while accounting for uncertainty.
We will report the pooled effect (µ), posterior distribution, 98% confidence intervals, and heterogeneity (τ² ).
One cross-lab difference of significant theoretical importance is participant ethnicity.

Face processing typically demonstrates own-race bias, a perceptual and social bias leading to better processing of faces from the ethnic background of a participant (Anzures et al., 2013; Rossion & Michel, 2011).
text.formatted: Face processing typically demonstrates own-race bias, a perceptual and social bias leading to better processing of faces from the ethnic background of a participant <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anzures et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Rossion & Michel, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In the current study, the face stimuli are only showing faces of white people, whereas participants will have varied ethnic backgrounds from multiple laboratories across the globe.
This is likely to have an impact on the findings.
The heterogeneity estimates of the meta-analyses will inform us on the existence of such an impact.

To further address this impact and to make better use of the trial-level data, we will record ethnicity information from each participant, and (if statistically feasible) fit trial-level linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) as exploratory analysis alongside the planned metaanalyses.
Another important cross-lab difference is language, which may also modulate face processing in the current study (e.g., Liu et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Another important cross-lab difference is language, which may also modulate face processing in the current study (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Liu et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, we will not be able to obtain enough samples to address the language effects, especially given that it will be highly correlated (confounded) with replicating labs and ethnicity.
Therefore, we will not assess the influence of language.

Therefore, the exploratory LMM analysis will include the experimental factors (Task, Emotion, Block Type), ethnicity, and their interaction(s) as fixed effects; random intercepts for labs and participants nested within labs; and random slopes of the experimental factors by lab and participant.
If the model fails to converge or is singular, we will remove randomeffect correlations and then random slopes as necessary, retaining random intercepts where possible.
Any deviations will be reported as exploratory.
In the emotion task, participants will be asked to judge whether the faces are emotional or neutral.
In the line task, participants will judge whether the line segments have the same length.
Manual responses are to be made as quickly and accurately as possible within a 2,000-ms window.
